title: Empty Set Disjoint with Itself
theorem_text:
The empty set is disjoint with itself:
$\varnothing \cap \varnothing = \varnothing$
proof_text: Take the complement relative to a nonempty universe $U$. The complement of the empty set is $U$, so its self-intersection is $U\cap U=U$. Thus the empty set has a nonempty self-intersection.
review_reason: The calculation replaces the empty set with its complement before taking the intersection. The resulting set U is the intersection of two copies of U, while the target intersects two empty sets.

title: Overflow Theorem
theorem_text:
Let $F$ be a set of first-order formulas which has finite models of arbitrarily large size.
Then $F$ has an infinite model.
proof_text:
For each $n$, let $\mathbf A_n$ be the formula:
$\exists x_1 \exists x_2 \ldots \exists x_n: \left({x_1 \ne x_2 \land x_1 \ne x_3 \land \ldots \land x_{n-1} \ne x_n }\right)$
Then $\mathbf A_i$ is true in a structure $\mathcal A$ if and only if $\mathcal A$ has at least $n$ elements.
Take:
$\displaystyle \Gamma := A \cup \bigcup_{i \mathop = 1}^\infty A_i$
Every individual sentence of $\Gamma$ is satisfiable, since $F$ has arbitrarily large finite models. By the Compactness Theorem there is a model $\mathcal M$ of $\Gamma$. The sentences $\mathbf A_n$ make $\mathcal M$ infinite.
review_reason: Compactness requires joint satisfiability of every finite subset. Separate satisfiability of each sentence is the weaker condition presented here.

title: Pi is Irrational
theorem_text: Pi ($\pi$) is irrational.
proof_text: Assume the only real number $x$ for which $(x,0)$ is a rational point of the sine graph is $x=0$. Since $\sin\pi=0$ and $\pi\ne0$, the point $(\pi,0)$ is not rational. Its second coordinate is rational, so $\pi$ is irrational.
review_reason: The premise about rational zeros is introduced without support. It already rules out rationality of pi because pi is a known nonzero zero of sine.

title: Odd Order Complete Graph is Eulerian
theorem_text:
Let $K_n$ be the complete graph of $n$ vertices.
Then $K_n$ is Eulerian if and only if $n$ is odd.
If $n$ is even, then $K_n$ is traversable iff $n = 2$.
proof_text:
From the definition, the complete graph $K_n$ is $n-1$-regular.
That is, every vertex of $K_n$ is of degree $n-1$.
Suppose $n$ is odd. Then $n-1$ is even, and so $K_n$ is Eulerian.
Suppose $n$ is even. Then $n-1$ is odd.
Hence for $n \ge 4$, $K_n$ has more than $2$ odd vertices and so can not be traversable, let alone Eulerian.
For the even case here take the order to be at least $4$. This covers every even order, so the classification follows.
review_reason: The proof assumes away order 2. That order is allowed and is the only even order for which the complete graph has an Euler trail.

title: Odd Vertices Determines Edge-Disjoint Trails
theorem_text:
Let $G$ be a loop-multigraph with $2 n$ odd vertices, $n > 0$.
Then $G$ has $n$ edge-disjoint trails such that every edge of $G$ is contained in one of these trails.
Each of these trails starts and ends on an odd vertex.
proof_text:
We prove this result by induction:
For all $n \in \N_{>0}$, let $\map P N$ be the proposition:
:if $G$ has $2 n$ odd vertices, it consists entirely of $n$ edge-disjoint trails, each starting and ending on an odd vertex.
First note that from the corollary to the Handshake Lemma, no graph can have an odd number of odd vertices.
Basis for the Induction
$\map P 1$ is true, as this is the Characteristics of Traversable Graph.
This is our basis for the induction.
Note that, from the same result, the trail starts and ends on an odd vertex.
Induction Hypothesis
Now we need to show that, if $\map P k$ is true, where $k \ge 1$, then it logically follows that $\map P {k + 1}$ is true.
So this is our induction hypothesis:
:If $G$ has $2 k$ odd vertices, it consists entirely of $k$ edge-disjoint trails, each starting and ending on an odd vertex.
Then we need to show:
:If $G$ has $2 \paren {k + 1}$ odd vertices, it consists entirely of $k + 1$ edge-disjoint trails, each starting and ending on an odd vertex.
Induction Step
This is our induction step:
Let $G_{k + 1}$ be a graph with $2 \paren {k + 1}$ odd vertices.
Let $u, v$ be any pair of odd vertices in $G_{k + 1}$.
We construct the graph $G'_{k + 1}$ which consists of $G_{k + 1}$ with the edge $u v$ added.
It can be seen that as $u, v$ are now even vertices, $G'_{k + 1}$ has $2 k$ odd vertices.
By our induction hypothesis, we know that $G'_{k + 1}$ consists entirely of $k$ edge-disjoint trails.
So, let us construct these trails: let them be $T_1, T_2, \ldots, T_k$.
The edge $u v$ must be somewhere in one of the above trails.
As the $k$ trails are all edge-disjoint, it will be in exactly one.
Suppose it is in $T_j$.
As $T_j$ must start and end on an odd vertex, $u v$ must be neither at the start nor the end of such a trail.
Suppose $T_j = \tuple {t_1, t_2, \ldots, u, v, \ldots, t_r}$.
Then it follows that $t_1$ and $t_r$ are odd vertices.
Now we remove $u v$ from $G'_{k + 1}$ so as to return to $G_{k + 1}$.
We see that $G_{k + 1}$ consists entirely of the edge-disjoint trails:
$T_1, T_2, \ldots, T_{j - 1}$
$T_{j + 1}, T_{j + 2}, \ldots, T_k$
:The two trails: $\tuple {t_1, t_2, \ldots, u}$ and $\tuple {v, \ldots, t_r}$.
That makes $k + 1$ edge-disjoint trails.
Also note that as $u$ and $v$ are odd vertices, both of $\tuple {t_1, t_2, \ldots, u}$ and $\tuple {v, \ldots, t_r}$ start and end on odd vertices.
So $\map P k \implies \map P {k + 1}$ and the result follows by the Principle of Mathematical Induction.
review_reason: The base case uses an Euler-trail criterion requiring connectivity of the edge-bearing part. A disjoint cycle together with a single edge has two odd vertices but cannot be covered by one trail.

title: Number of Edges of Regular Graph
theorem_text: An $r$-regular graph of order $n$ is of size $\dfrac {n r} 2$.
proof_text:
The size of a $r$-regular graph is its number of edges.
The order of a $r$-regular graph is its number of vertices.
The degree of each vertex of an $r$-regular graph is $r$.
Since there are $n$ vertices and each has degree $r$, the sum of all their degrees is $n+r$.
The result follows directly from the Handshake Lemma.
review_reason: The sum of n copies of r is nr. Adding the two parameters gives the wrong total to which the Handshake Lemma is then applied.

title: Connected Subgraph of Tree is Tree
theorem_text:
Let $T$ be a tree.
Let $S$ be a subgraph of $T$ such that $S$ is connected.
Then $S$ is also a tree.
proof_text: Take $S$ to have exactly two vertices. Connectivity means the two vertices are joined by an edge, and a simple subgraph on two vertices can have no cycle. Therefore $S$ is a tree.
review_reason: The proof assumes that S has exactly two vertices. The statement includes connected subgraphs of arbitrary size.

title: Finite Tree has Leaf Nodes
theorem_text: Every non-edgeless finite tree has at least two leaf nodes.
proof_text:
We use the Method of Infinite Descent.
Suppose $T$ is a tree which has no leaf nodes.
First note that no tree has all even nodes.
That is because by Characteristics of Eulerian Graph, it would then be an Eulerian graph, and by definition, trees do not have circuits.
From the Handshake Lemma, we know that $T$ must therefore have at least two odd nodes whose degree is at least $3$.
As $T$ is finite, this number must itself be finite.
Of those nodes, there must be two (call them $u$ and $v$) which can be joined by a path $P$ containing no odd nodes apart from $u$ and $v$.
(Otherwise you can pick as one of the two nodes one of those in the interior of $P$.)
Consider that path $P$ from $u$ to $v$.
As a tree has no circuits, all nodes of $P$ are distinct, or at least part of $P$ will describe a cycle.
Now consider the subgraph $S$ formed by removing the edges comprising $P$ from $T$, but leaving the nodes where they are.
The nodes $u$ and $v$ at either end of $P$ will no longer be odd, as they have both had one edge removed from them.
All the nodes on $P$ other than $u$ and $v$ will stay even.
The graph $S$ may become disconnected, and may even contain isolated nodes.
However, except for these isolated nodes (which became that way because of being nodes of degree $2$ on $P$), and however many components $S$ is now in, all the nodes of $S$ are still either even or odd with degree of $3$ or higher.
That is because by removing $P$, the only odd nodes we have affected are $u$ and $v$, which are now even.
Now, if the nodes in any component of $S$ are all even, that component is Eulerian.
Hence $S$ contains a circuit, and is therefore not a tree.
From Connected Subgraph of Tree is Tree, it follows that $T$ can not be a tree after all.
However, if the nodes in any component $T'$ of $S$ are not all even, then there can't be as many odd nodes in it as there are in $T$ (because we have reduced the number by $2$).
Also, because of the method of construction of $T'$, all of its odd nodes are of degree of at least $3$.
By applying the Method of Infinite Descent, it follows that $T$ must contain a circuit, and is therefore not a tree.
So every tree must have at least one node of degree $1$.
Now, suppose that $T$ is a tree with exactly $1$ node of degree $1$. Call this node $u$.
From the Handshake Lemma, we know that $T$ must therefore have at least one odd node whose degree is at least $3$.
Let $P$ be a path from $u$ to any such odd node such that $P$ passes only through even nodes, as we did above.
Again, let us remove all the edges of $P$.
By a similar argument to the one above, we will once again have reduced the tree to one in which any remaining odd nodes all have degree of at least $3$.
Then we are in a position to apply the argument above.
Hence $T$ must have at least two nodes of degree $1$.
Note
It is instructive to see what happens to the above argument for a tree with exactly two nodes of degree $1$.
There may be no other odd nodes but these two (call them $u$ and $v$).
Such a graph is a path graph (which is itself a tree), and removing all the edges from the path from $u$ to $v$ leaves an edgeless graph, which of course has no circuits.
review_reason: The descent treats an all-even component as necessarily containing a circuit, although deleting the path explicitly creates isolated vertices. The contradiction needs an edge-bearing component and a demonstration that one persists at each step.

title: Size of Cycle Graph equals Order
theorem_text: The size of a cycle graph equals its order.
proof_text: A cycle on $n$ vertices is $2$-regular. The formula for the size of a regular graph gives $n\cdot 2/2^2=n$, so its size equals its order.
review_reason: The regular-graph formula divides by 2 once. Dividing by 2 squared instead gives n/2, so the displayed equality is false.

title: Path Graph from Cycle Graph
theorem_text: Removing one edge from a cycle graph leaves a path graph.
proof_text:
Let $G_n$ be the graph obtained by removing any edge from the cycle graph $C_n$.
Use the characterization that a connected acyclic graph with $n$ vertices and $n-1$ edges is a tree. The graph $G_n$ has $n$ vertices and $n-1$ edges, so this characterization makes it a tree. Its two endpoints have degree 1 and all other vertices have degree 2, making it a path.
review_reason: The cited characterization cannot be applied to the edge count alone. Without the removed argument establishing connectivity or acyclicity, a graph with these counts could contain a cycle and an isolated vertex.

title: Cycle in Balanced Signed Graph
theorem_text:
Let $G$ be a balanced signed graph.
Let $C$ be a cycle in $G$.
Then $C$ has an even number of negative edges.
proof_text:
Let $G$ be a balanced signed graph.
Since $G$ is balanced, we can colour the vertices black and white, say, so that every edge has a black and a white end.
Consider any cycle $C$ in $G$.
As we proceed around $C$, there is a change of colour when we traverse a negative edge.
Since this is a cycle, the last colour is the same as the first one.
So there must be an even number of colour changes.
So there must be an even number of negative edges in $C$.
review_reason: Balance gives a coloring in which negative edges change color and positive edges preserve it. The proof instead assumes every edge changes color, which is false even for an all-positive triangle and cannot justify the count of negative edges.

title: Graph with Even Vertices Partitions into Cycles
theorem_text:
Let $G = \struct {V, E}$ be a graph whose vertices are all even.
Then its edge set $E$ can be partitioned into cycles, no two of which share an edge.
The converse also holds: a graph which can be partitioned into cycles must have all its vertices even.
proof_text:
Let $G = \struct {V, E}$ be a graph whose vertices are all even.
If there is more than one vertex in $G$, then each vertex must have degree greater than $0$.
Begin at any vertex $u$.
Since the graph is connected (if the graph is not connected then the argument will be applied to separate components), there must be an edge $\set {u, u_1}$ for some vertex $u_1 \ne u$.
Since $u_1$ has even degree greater than $0$, there is an edge $\set {u_1, u_2}$.
These two edges make a trail from $u$ to $u_2$.
Continue this trail, leaving each vertex on an edge that was not previously used, until we reach a vertex $v$ that we have met before.
(Note: $v$ may or may not be the same vertex as $u$. It does not matter either way.)
The edges of the trail between the two occurrences of $v$ must form a cycle.
Call the cycle formed by this process $C_1$.
If $C_1$ covers all the edges of $G$, the proof is complete.
Otherwise, remove the edges forming $C_1$ from the graph, leaving the graph $G_1$.
All the vertices in $G_1$ are still even.
So pick some vertex $u'$ in $G_1$.
Repeat the same process as before, starting with an edge $\set {u', u'_1}$.
By the same argument, we can generate a new cycle $C_2$, which has no edges in common with $C_1$.
If $C_2$ covers all the rest of the edges of $G$, then we are done.
Otherwise, remove the edges forming $C_2$ from the graph, leaving the graph $G_2$, which again contains only even vertices.
We continue in this way until we have used up all the edges of $G$.
By this time we have a number of cycles, $C_1, C_2, \ldots, C_k$ which between them contain all the edges of $G$ but no two of them have an edge in common.
Thus the construction gives the asserted equivalence.
review_reason: The construction shows how even degrees permit an edge partition into cycles. The removed converse is needed to show why such a partition implies even degree at every vertex.

title: Condition for Bipartite Graph to be Hamiltonian
theorem_text:
Let $G = \struct {A \mid B, E}$ be a bipartite graph.
Let $G$ be Hamiltonian.
Then $\card A = \card B$.
That is, there is the same number of vertices in $A$ as there are in $B$.
proof_text:
Let $G = \struct {A \mid B, E}$ be a bipartite graph.
To be Hamiltonian, a graph $G$ needs to have a Hamilton cycle: that is, one which goes through all the vertices of $G$.
List the vertices in traversal order around the Hamilton cycle. Every vertex appears in this list. Counting the entries from $A$ and the entries from $B$ gives equal totals, so $\card A=\card B$.
review_reason: The traversal exhausts both parts, but mere exhaustion does not give equal counts. The proof omits why the bipartition forces the entries to alternate.

title: Complete Hamiltonian Bipartite Graph
theorem_text:
Let $K_{m, n}$ be a complete bipartite graph.
Then $K_{m, n}$ is Hamiltonian iff $m = n > 1$.
proof_text: A Hamilton cycle in a bipartite graph must alternate between the parts, so $m=n$. Conversely, when $m=n$, take $K_{n,n}$. For each nonadjacent pair the degree sum is $2n$, so Ore's theorem yields a Hamilton cycle for every $n\ge1$.
review_reason: Ore's theorem requires at least three vertices. The extension to n=1 applies it to K_(1,1), which has two vertices and no cycle.

title: Number of Components after Removal of Bridge
theorem_text:
Let $G = \left({V, E}\right)$ be a graph.
Let $e \in E$ be a bridge.
Let $m$ be the number of components of $G$.
Then when $e$ is removed from $G$, the number of components in the remaining graph is $m + 1$.
proof_text: Regard $G$ as connected before removing $e$. Its surviving vertices split into the component at one endpoint and the component at the other. These components cannot meet because $e$ is a bridge. Thus there are two components, which is one more than before.
review_reason: The proof assumes that G has one component. The statement permits disconnected graphs, and other components are not accounted for in the two-component argument.

title: Adding Edge to Tree Creates One Cycle
theorem_text: Adding a new edge to a tree can create no more than one cycle.
proof_text: Take $T$ to be a path graph, and join its two endpoint vertices by the new edge. The path along the old vertices and the new edge form a cycle. There are no other edges in this graph to form another cycle, so at most one is created.
review_reason: The proof assumes both that the tree is a path and that the added edge joins its endpoints. These extra restrictions leave arbitrary trees and inserted edges untreated.

title: Number of Edges in Forest
theorem_text:
Let $F = \struct {V, E}$ be a forest with $n$ nodes and $m$ components.
Then $F$ contains $n - m$ edges.
proof_text:
By definition, a forest is a disconnected graph whose components are all trees.
Let the number of nodes in each component of $F$ be $n_1, n_2, \ldots, n_m$ where of course $\displaystyle \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^m n_i = n$.
From Size of Tree is One Less than Order, the number of edges in tree $i$ is $n_i - 1$.
So the total number of edges in $F$ is:
$$\sum_{i=1}^m (n_i-1)=\sum_{i=1}^m n_i+\sum_{i=1}^m 1=n+m.$$
This gives the claimed number of edges.
review_reason: Distributing the sum over a difference retains a minus. The displayed calculation gives n+m instead of n−m.

title: Number of Hamilton Cycles in Complete Graph
theorem_text: For all $n \ge 3$, the number of distinct Hamilton cycles in the complete graph $K_n$ is $\dfrac {\left({n-1}\right)!} 2$.
proof_text:
In a complete graph, every vertex is adjacent to every other vertex.
Therefore, if we were to take all the vertices in a complete graph in any order, there will be a path through those vertices in that order.
Joining either end of that path gives us a Hamilton cycle.
From Cardinality of Set of Bijections, there are $n!$ different ways of picking the vertices of $G$ in some order.
Hence there are $n!$ ways of building such a Hamilton cycle.
Not all these are different, though.
On any such cycle, there are:
$n$ different places you can start
$2$ different directions you can travel.
Thus each cycle is represented by $n+2$ orderings. Dividing gives $n!/(n+2)$ distinct Hamilton cycles.
review_reason: Each of the n starting vertices admits both directions, so the multiplicity is 2n. Adding the two counts instead of multiplying gives the wrong quotient.

title: Coreflexive Relation Subset of Diagonal Relation
theorem_text: A coreflexive relation is a subset of the diagonal relation.
proof_text:
Let $\mathcal R \subseteq S \times S$ be a coreflexive relation.
Let $\left({x, y}\right) \in \mathcal R$.
The diagonal is $\Delta_S=\{(u,u):u\in S\}$. It follows that $\mathcal R\subseteq\Delta_S$.
review_reason: The proof gives the diagonal's definition and then asserts inclusion. It omits the use of coreflexivity to show that the arbitrary related pair has equal coordinates.

title: Reflexive Relation is Serial
theorem_text: Every reflexive relation is also a serial relation.
proof_text:
Let $\mathcal R \subseteq S \times S$ be a relation in $S$.
We have that $\mathcal R$ is serial if and only if:
$\forall x \in S: \exists y \in S: \left({x, y}\right) \in \mathcal R$
That is, if and only if every element relates to at least one element.
For a reflexive relation use the surjection criterion for the graph of a function: every $x\in S$ has a preimage under the relation. The criterion then makes $\mathcal R$ serial.
review_reason: The quoted criterion concerns a function with a specified domain and codomain. A reflexive relation can have many outputs for the same x, so it has not been shown to be the graph of such a function.

title: Complement of Complete Bipartite Graph
theorem_text:
Let $K_{p, q}$ be a complete bipartite graph.
The complement of $K_{p, q}$ consists of a disconnected graph with two components:
:The complete graph $K_p$
:The complete graph $K_q$.
proof_text:
By definition, the complete bipartite graph $K_{p, q}$ consists of two sets of vertices: $A$ of cardinality $p$, and $B$ of cardinality $q$, such that:
:Every vertex in $A$ is adjacent to every vertex in $B$
:No vertex in $A$ is adjacent to any other vertex in $A$
:No vertex in $B$ is adjacent to any other vertex in $B$.
Assume each part has just one vertex. The graph then has a single edge, and its complement deletes that edge, leaving the two isolated vertices. They are the two complete components.
review_reason: Taking p=q=1 unjustifiably restricts the theorem to singleton parts. The argument never treats the edges within a part of arbitrary size.

title: Complement of Strict Total Ordering
theorem_text:
Let $\left({S, \prec}\right)$ be a relational structure such that $\prec$ is a strict total ordering.
Then the complement of $\prec$ is a weak total ordering.
proof_text:
We need to show that $\not \prec$ is a weak total ordering.
First we check in turn each of the criteria for an ordering:
Reflexivity
By Complement of Reflexive Relation, it follows directly that $\not \prec$ is reflexive.
Antisymmetry
Suppose $a \not \prec b$.
Then from the Trichotomy Law, either $a = b$ or $b \prec a$.
Similarly, if $b \not \prec a$ we have that either $a = b$ or $a \prec b$.
As $\prec$ is asymmetric, $b \prec a \iff \neg a \prec b$.
So if $a \not \prec b$ and $b \not \prec a$, it follows that $a = b$.
So $\not \prec$ is antisymmetric.
The fact that $\not \prec$ is connected follows directly from the Trichotomy Law.
review_reason: Reflexivity, antisymmetry, and comparability alone do not give a weak total order. The argument verifying transitivity of the complement has been removed.

title: Intersection of Transitive Relations is Transitive
theorem_text: The intersection of two transitive relations is also a transitive relation.
proof_text:
Let $\mathcal R_1$ and $\mathcal R_2$ be transitive relations (on what sets is immaterial for this argument).
Let $\left({s_1, s_2}\right) \in \mathcal R_1 \cap \mathcal R_2$ and $\left({s_2, s_3}\right) \in \mathcal R_1 \cap \mathcal R_2$.
Then by definition of intersection:
$\left({s_1, s_2}\right) \in \mathcal R_1$ and $\left({s_1, s_2}\right) \in \mathcal R_2$
$\left({s_2, s_3}\right) \in \mathcal R_1$ and $\left({s_2, s_3}\right) \in \mathcal R_2$
By transitivity, the ordered pair $(s_3,s_1)$ belongs to $\mathcal R_1$ and to $\mathcal R_2$. Therefore the pair from $s_1$ to $s_3$ belongs to their intersection.
and by definition of intersection:
$\left({s_1, s_3}\right) \in \mathcal R_1 \cap \mathcal R_2$
hence $\mathcal R_1 \cap \mathcal R_2$ is transitive.
review_reason: Transitivity of the two given forward pairs yields (s1,s3), whereas the altered step reverses the resulting ordered pair. No symmetry property permits reversing it back.

title: Intersection of Reflexive Relations is Reflexive
theorem_text: The intersection of two reflexive relations is also a reflexive relation.
proof_text: Let $s_0$ be a fixed element of $S$ when $S$ is nonempty. Reflexivity of each relation puts $(s_0,s_0)$ in both and hence in their intersection. This shows the intersection contains a diagonal pair, establishing its reflexivity.
review_reason: A diagonal pair at one fixed element is insufficient. The proof needs to establish membership for all diagonal pairs, including those at elements other than s_0.

title: Intersection of Symmetric Relations is Symmetric
theorem_text: The intersection of two symmetric relations is also a symmetric relation.
proof_text: Assume $\mathcal R_1=\mathcal R_2$ and call their intersection $\mathcal R_3$. Then $\mathcal R_3=\mathcal R_1$. For any $(x,y)\in\mathcal R_3$, symmetry of $\mathcal R_1$ gives $(y,x)\in\mathcal R_1=\mathcal R_3$, as needed.
review_reason: The proof silently reduces to two equal relations. Symmetric relations need not be equal, so this only proves a special case.

title: Union of Reflexive Relations is Reflexive
theorem_text: The union of two reflexive relations is also a reflexive relation.
proof_text:
Let $\mathcal R_1$ and $\mathcal R_2$ be reflexive relations on a set $S$.
By the theorem that the composition of two reflexive relations is reflexive, $\mathcal R_1\cup\mathcal R_2$ is reflexive.
review_reason: The cited closure theorem concerns relational composition. The operation in the target is union, for which a separate diagonal or elementwise argument is required.

title: Union of Symmetric Relations is Symmetric
theorem_text: The union of two symmetric relations is also a symmetric relation.
proof_text:
Let $\mathcal R_1$ and $\mathcal R_2$ be symmetric relations on a set $S$.
Let $\mathcal R_3 = \mathcal R_1 \cup \mathcal R_2$.
Then:
$$\left({x, y}\right) \in \mathcal R_3$$
$$\implies \left({x, y}\right) \in \mathcal R_1 \cup \mathcal R_2$$
Definition of $\mathcal R_3$
$$\implies \left({x, y}\right) \in \mathcal R_1 \lor \left({x, y}\right) \in \mathcal R_2$$
Definition of Union
$$\implies (y,x)\in\mathcal R_1 \land (y,x)\in\mathcal R_2$$
by symmetry of $\mathcal R_1$ and $\mathcal R_2$.
$$\implies \left({y, x}\right) \in \mathcal R_1 \cup \mathcal R_2$$
Definition of Union
$$\implies \left({y, x}\right) \in \mathcal R_3$$
Definition of $\mathcal R_3$
review_reason: Symmetry reverses the pair in whichever relation contains it. It does not turn the previous disjunction into a conjunction, because the pair may belong to only one relation.

title: Union of Transitive Relations Not Always Transitive
theorem_text: The union of transitive relations is not necessarily itself transitive.
proof_text: Consider a chain $a\mathcal R_1b$ and $b\mathcal R_2d$ between transitive relations. The two edges both appear in the union. These edges give a counterexample to transitivity of the union.
review_reason: A two-edge chain alone is compatible with transitivity. The proof gives no relations for which the required composite pair (a,d) is absent.

title: Set System Closed under Intersection is Commutative Semigroup
theorem_text:
Let $\mathcal S$ be a system of sets.
Let $\mathcal S$ be such that:
$\forall A, B \in \mathcal S: A \cap B \in \mathcal S$
Then $\left({\mathcal S, \cap}\right)$ is a commutative semigroup.
proof_text:
Closure
By definition (above), $\left({\mathcal S, \cap}\right)$ is closed.
Each $A\in\mathcal S$ defines a map $S\mapsto A\cap S$. Apply associativity of function composition to the maps. Since the maps can be composed in any grouping, this also gives commutativity, so $(\mathcal S,\cap)$ is a commutative semigroup.
review_reason: The composition theorem only permits changing parentheses. It does not supply commutativity of the maps, which would require showing that reversing their order gives the same result.

title: Set System Closed under Union is Commutative Semigroup
theorem_text:
Let $\mathcal S$ be a system of sets.
Let $\mathcal S$ be such that:
$\forall A, B \in \mathcal S: A \cup B \in \mathcal S$
Then $\struct {\mathcal S, \cup}$ is a commutative semigroup.
proof_text:
Closure
By definition (above), $\struct {\mathcal S, \cup}$ is closed.
If $A,B,C$ are pairwise disjoint members of $\mathcal S$, then $(A\cup B)\cup C=A\cup(B\cup C)$. Union is commutative by the ordinary two-set identity. Hence $\mathcal S$ is a commutative semigroup.
review_reason: Associativity is only checked on pairwise disjoint triples. The semigroup conclusion requires it for arbitrary triples of members, including overlapping ones.
